facts.title: Punk Rock (1976) – Reactionary Not Revolutionary; Return to Short Sharp Songs; The Rock Great Schism
facts.body: Punk rock emerged almost simultaneously in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia in 1976. It was a reactionary backlash against how complicated and artsy rock had become — a return to short, sharp, melodic songs, but faster, louder, more anti-establishment. The Ramones were the most important early spreaders of the gospel from 1974 onward. British punk was less artsy and more political, concerned with the class system. 1976 was to rock what the Great Schism of 1054 was to the Catholic Church — it split rock into two mostly independent and autonomous streams that ran parallel, crossing over only rarely, each disavowing the other. "It wasn't revolutionary at all. It was reactionary."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Guide to Genres: Part 1
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: UK Scene (Fall 1976) – Concentrated London Festival
facts.body: The UK punk scene emerged in the fall of 1976 with a similarly small number of participants. Nearly every London punk could fit into a single venue, the 100 Club on Oxford Street, which hosted a two-night music festival with an official capacity of 350, though there was reportedly ample space to move around. "The UK punk scene started with a similar number in the fall of 1976. Pretty much every London punk fit into a single club on Oxford Street for a two-night music festival."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Chris Cornell: 6 Degrees of Separation
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: British Adoption of "Punk" (Summer 1976)
facts.body: British writers like Nick Kent and aspiring managers such as Malcolm McLaren discovered the nascent New York scene and eagerly adopted the term "punk." They imported it into the UK, where it coincided with the rise of bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash, leading to the "British punk rock explosion" that began in the summer of 1976 and officially christened their movement "punk rock." "It wasn't long before British writers and scene stars happened upon what was going on in New York. And they really liked the word punk."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Shift from Curiosity to Mainstream Force (1976)
facts.body: Before December 1st, 1976, punk rock was a "weird curiosity" confined to the fringes of the mainstream press. Following the Sex Pistols' infamous 117-second live TV interview on the *Today* show, the genre exploded into national conversation in the UK, becoming widely discussed, albeit often negatively. This controversy, however, fueled its popularity, transforming it into "the biggest and most dangerous thing in the world." "Suddenly the whole nation was talking about punk rock and how awful it was."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: English Rock Turning Point (1976)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols' gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4, 1976, despite being a financial failure with fewer than 50 attendees, proved to be a pivotal turning point for English rock. The concert inspired future members of significant bands like the Buzzcocks, Pet Shop Boys, Joy Division, and New Order, sparking the widespread adoption and creation of punk rock across England. "Didn't seem like much of the time, but this failed money losing gig became a turning point for English rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: 1976 Explosion
facts.body: The year 1976 is identified as the "big bang" or explosion of punk rock, which served as the foundational event leading to all subsequent alternative rock music. "We're picking 1976 as our starting year because that was the year of the punk rock explosion, the big bang that led to all the Alt Rock that followed."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 50 Biggest All-Time Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders: Part 1
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: "Great Explosion" of 1976
facts.body: The year 1976 is identified as the "Great Punk Rock Explosion," a pivotal event from which nearly all modern alternative music originates, akin to a "big bang" for the genre. "Our starting point is 1976, the year of the Great Punk Rock Explosion, the thing from which practically all of today's alternative music emanates."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 50 Biggest Alt-Rock One-Hit Wonders of All Time: Part 2 (40-31)
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: 1976-1977 Seismic Shift
facts.body: The birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977 are described as a seismic period in music history, paralleling the transformative years of alt-rock in 1990-1991. "They are every bit as seismic as what we saw with the birth and rise of punk in 1976 and 1977."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 11
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Growth and Organization (1976)
facts.body: By September 1976, hundreds of punk rock bands had formed across Britain, attracting regular followings and playing gigs wherever possible. This growth led to the organization of larger events, such as the 100 Club Punk Rock Festival, to assess the burgeoning scene. "Still, by September of 1976, there were hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of these punk rock bands all over Britain."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Cultural Storm Example (1976-1982)
facts.body: Punk Rock is cited as an example of a "perfect cultural storm," with its period of significant impact and influence spanning from 1976 to 1982. "Think of Punk Rock from 76 to 82."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Lesser Free Trade Hall Concert (1976) – Captured on Bootleg, Historically Pivotal
facts.body: The influential Sex Pistols concert at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester in 1976 was captured on a bootleg recording. The show is considered one of the most historically significant concerts in rock history, credited with directly inspiring the formation of multiple major post-punk bands. "The influential Sex Pistols concert at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in 1976 was captured on a bootleg."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Another Look At Bootlegging: Part 2
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Catalyst for British Punk Rock Explosion (Summer 1976)
facts.body: The emergence of the Sex Pistols was concurrent with the "British punk rock explosion," which commenced in the summer of 1976. Along with The Clash and other groups, their rise led to the term "punk rock" being imported from New York to the UK and used to define this new, vibrant British musical movement. "This coincided with the rise of the sex pistols and the clash in all the other groups who were really part of the British punk rock explosion which began in the summer of 1976."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
facts.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Perceived Uncompromising Ideology (1976-1977)
facts.body: In the nascent stages of British punk, particularly around 1976 and 1977, The Sex Pistols were widely regarded as the most uncompromising and ideologically pure of all the bands in the movement. This perception stood in stark contrast to other bands like The Clash, who faced criticism for signing major label deals. "The clash was seen as the most uncompromising and the most ideologically pure of all the British punk bands."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Lesser Free Trade Hall Gig (1976)
facts.body: On Friday, June 4, 1976, just after 7:30 PM, the Sex Pistols played a pivotal gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester. Despite selling tickets for only 50 pence, fewer than 50 people attended, making it a "failed money losing gig." Nonetheless, this concert proved to be a transformative moment for English rock, as the small audience included future members of influential bands such as the Buzzcocks, Pet Shop Boys, Joy Division, and New Order. "Didn't seem like much of the time, but this failed money losing gig became a turning point for English rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
facts.body: Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious were among the British punk figures who attended The Ramones' influential gig at the Roundhouse in London. They were "transformed by what they saw and heard," learning a lesson that contributed to the British punk rock explosion. "Johnny Rotten and Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols were there."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: 100 Club Punk Rock Festival Performance (September 20, 1976)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols performed on the first night of Britain's first official punk rock festival at the 100 Club on Oxford Street, London. This festival, also featuring The Clash and The Damned, was crucial in making punk rock no longer a secret in the UK. "Here's part of the pistol set from that very first night. I see even sex pistols going."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Record Label Controversies (1976-1977)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols, managed by Malcolm McLaren's Glitter Best, first secured a deal with EMI Records. However, they were soon dropped due to their controversial nature and were essentially paid to leave. Next, they signed with A&M Records, a contract that notoriously lasted only five days before the band was again paid to go away. Their third and final deal was with Virgin Records, and this one "stuck," allowing the Sex Pistols to become a sensation and indeed challenge the British establishment.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: First Rehearsals and Demos (July 1976)
facts.body: The band first rehearsed and made their initial demos in July 1976 at Number 6 Denmark Street in London, an area also known as the UK's Tin Pan Alley. The members also lived together on the upper floor of this location, which is now recognized as a site of important cultural significance in the UK. "number 6 Denmark Street was where the sex pistols first rehearsed and where they made their first demos. They also lived together on the upper floor. This is now considered to be a site of important cultural significance in the UK."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Music Questions People Almost Never Ask
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Bill Grundy Interview (1976)
facts.body: On December 1, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on Bill Grundy's afternoon talk show as last-minute substitutes. The band arrived drunk and surly, leading to an infamous on-air interview filled with obscenities. This controversial broadcast, likened to the "Janet Jackson Nipplegate scandal of its day," transformed the Sex Pistols from mere curiosities into national and international sensations.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: New Rock Secrets
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: TV Appearance Controversy (December 1, 1976)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols appeared on a popular TV show on December 1, 1976, and used "a couple of bad words," which caused a major scandal throughout Britain. "They had been in a popular TV show the night before and had said a couple of bad words. Now this had caused quite a scandal. All of Britain was talking about it."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The 500th Show!
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Signing with EMI (1976) - Subversive Victory
facts.body: On October 8, 1976, the Sex Pistols signed a deal with EMI records for £40,000, which was considered a fortune at the time. This move was admired by the punk community, who saw it not as selling out, but as a "major subversive victory" for managing to "swindle such a huge amount of money from a gullible multinational major record label." "And the home of the Beatles no less. This was considered to be a major subversive victory for the punk rock cause."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Infamous "Today" TV Appearance (1976) - National Scandal
facts.body: On December 1, 1976, the Sex Pistols were booked as last-minute substitute guests on the bland "Today" chat show after Queen cancelled due to Freddie Mercury needing a dentist. Lured to the studio with champagne and beer, the band members were "heavily toasted" upon arrival. The two-minute interview, which featured multiple instances of swearing on live television, including the word "f**k," immediately became a gigantic national scandal, leading to headlines condemning "punk rock scum" and "the filth in the fury." "This two minutes has gone down in history as one of the most legendary rock and roll television appearances ever."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Bill Grundy TV Incident – December 1976
facts.body: Following their appearance with Bill Grundy on television in December 1976, the Sex Pistols became the recognizable face of punk rock in Britain. This event caused them to be viewed by many as symbolic of everything perceived as wrong with Britain's youth, igniting a media storm comparable to the intense public fascination around an unnaturally huge boy band or pop star today. "Ever since they were running with Bill Grundy on the tally back in December of 1976, the Pistols had become the face of punk rock in Britain."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 5
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Malcolm McLaren's Use of "New Wave" (1976)
facts.body: In late 1976, Sex Pistols manager Malcolm McLaren, described as a "very artsy guy," was quoted in *Melody Maker* magazine using the term "new wave." He applied it to bands that, while related to punk and sharing its core "seam," did not necessarily embody a strictly "punk" sound, thus helping to popularize the term. "Later that year, late 76, a story in Melody Maker magazine quoted Sex Pistols Manager Malcolm McLaren, very artsy guy. And he was using the term and applying it to bands that were related to punk, part of the same seamst punk, but not necessarily sounding that punk at all."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Pre-Recording Status in 1976
facts.body: By April 1976, when the Ramones' debut album was released, the Sex Pistols "existed but hadn't recorded yet." They were part of the nascent British punk scene that was inspired by the New York sound. "The sex pistols existed but hadn't recorded yet."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Original Ramones
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: TV Show Scandal (December 1, 1976)
facts.body: The Sex Pistols appeared on a popular television program where they used "bad words," leading to a significant scandal across Britain. This incident was widely discussed and served as a catalyst for future musicians, inspiring Declan McManus (later Elvis Costello) to pursue a career in music. "All of Britain was talking about it. Terrible, terrible. These young men on TV."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Manchester Gig Inspiration (Spring 1976)
facts.body: A performance by the Sex Pistols in Manchester, though described as "terrible" by attendees Bernie and Peter, was nonetheless found to be "great" in its raw energy. This concert directly inspired Bernie and Peter to form their own band, which would eventually become Joy Division. "He says, they were terrible. I thought they were great. I wanted to get up there and be terrible too."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Infamous `Today` Show Appearance (December 1, 1976)
facts.body: On December 1, 1976, the Sex Pistols were a last-minute replacement for Queen on the British tea time chat show `Today`. Both the band, their entourage, and host Bill Grundy had been drinking, leading to two minutes of shocking, profanity-laced television that became one of the most scandalous moments in British TV history. "So someone in desperation reached out to the Sex Pistols. Could you whip your on the show with Bill Grundy this afternoon? Absolutely. There."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Weird and Shocking Rockers
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Tabloid Reaction to TV Appearance (December 2, 1976)
facts.body: The day after their `Today` show appearance, British tabloids ran front-page stories on the "disgusting, shocking punks who swore on TV," with the Daily Mail famously headlining, "The Filth and the Fury." "The next morning, December 2nd, 1976, the British tabloids led with the story of the disgusting, shocking punks who swore on TV. The most famous headline was one that appeared in huge type on the front of the Daily Mail, the filth and the fury."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Weird and Shocking Rockers
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

facts.title: Bill Grundy Show Appearance (December 1, 1976)
facts.body: Malcolm McLaren, the band's manager, was contacted by Bill Grundy's office for a last-minute appearance on the "Today" show after Queen cancelled. The band and their entourage, already heavily inebriated from bottles of wine consumed in the limo, were escorted onto the live TV set at 6:15pm. During the interview, members of the band engaged in swearing on air, leading to Bill Grundy's TV career ending by 6:18pm and the country being shocked. "Someone in Bill Grundy's office got a hold of Malcolm McLaren, the manager of a new group called the Sex Pistols, who had just released their debut single a week earlier."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: The Sex Pistols

"Malcolm McLaren, who was still the manager of the Sex Bistels at the time, peppered some of his interviews with this term."

Their initial group was called Warsaw, which subsequently evolved into Joy Division, and later New Order. "If they could do it, maybe we could."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Inspired by Sex Pistols Gig (1976)
facts.body: A group that would soon be known as Joy Division was inspired after attending a Sex Pistols show in Manchester. "Still in Manchester, a group soon to be called Joy Division was inspired by a sex pistols show."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 5
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Inspired by Sex Pistols Gig (1976)
facts.body: Future members of Joy Division were among the attendees at the Sex Pistols' seminal concert at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4, 1976. This event, despite attracting fewer than 50 people, profoundly impacted those present and contributed to the burgeoning English rock scene. "In the audience that night were future members of the buscocks and the pet shop boys and joy division and new order."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 5
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Part of British Punk Rock Explosion (Summer 1976)
facts.body: The Clash's ascent coincided with the "British punk rock explosion," which ignited in the summer of 1976. Alongside the Sex Pistols and other bands, they were central to this movement, leading to the adoption of the term "punk rock" from New York to christen this new British musical phenomenon. "This coincided with the rise of the sex pistols and the clash in all the other groups who were really part of the British punk rock explosion which began in the summer of 1976."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
facts.body: Members of the newly formed Clash, including Joe Strummer, were present at The Ramones' July 4, 1976 gig at the Roundhouse in London. Strummer recounted how they got backstage by forming a "human chain" through a window to meet The Ramones, describing it as a "really great punk rock moment." "Members of the newly formed clash, Chrissy Hind of the still unformed pretenders, the damn who would become the first British punk band to release a record, Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: 100 Club Punk Rock Festival Performance (September 20, 1976)
facts.body: The Clash performed at Britain's first official punk rock festival held at the 100 Club on Oxford Street, London. This festival, alongside the Sex Pistols and The Damned, marked a turning point where punk rock became widely known. "This was the site of Britain's first official punk rock festival."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Breaking Gender Stereotypes (1976-1977)
facts.body: When the Talking Heads moved to New York in 1976 and 1977, people were shocked to discover their bass player was a woman, as this was considered "unladylike" and almost as scandalous as a woman playing drums at the time. Tina Weymouth's presence as a female bassist challenged and broke down numerous stereotypes and preconceptions. "When the talking heads moved to New York, people were shocked to find that their bass player was a woman."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Regeneration in West Berlin (May 1976)
facts.body: In late May 1976, Iggy Pop moved to West Berlin with David Bowie to escape their destructive lifestyles in Los Angeles and to regenerate among the city's diverse community of bohemians, weirdos, drug addicts, prostitutes, and transsexuals. This move, prompted by Bowie's heart attack scare in the fall of 1976, led both artists to seriously clean up their acts and embark on an incredibly creative period. "So in late May 1976, Bowie and Iggy moved to West Berlin to regenerate in the company of the Bohemians and weirdos and drug addicts and prostitutes and transsexuals who lived there."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.title: Move to West Berlin with David Bowie (Post-1976)
facts.body: Iggy Pop, seeking sobriety, moved to West Berlin with David Bowie after Bowie's period of intense drug addiction and paranoia. They both aimed to clean up and dry out in the city. "It wasn't until he and Iggy Pop had a moment of clarity and decided that they needed to move to West Berlin to clean up, get sober and dry out."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History 2
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.title: "Sister Midnight" Performance on Dina (1976)
facts.body: During an appearance on Dina Shore's talk show in 1976, Iggy Pop performed his "eerie song sister midnight," twitching his way through the performance. In the post-performance chat, Shore asked him about his stage antics of crawling across glass, to which he replied, "I've had treatment for that."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 56 - Talk Shows of the 1970s
facts.name: Iggy Pop

facts.title: Contribution to Low (1976)
facts.body: Iggy Pop, who was living with David Bowie in Berlin during the recording of "Low," contributed backing vocals to some of the songs and assisted Bowie in various other recording processes for the album.

facts.title: Soho Newspaper Criticism (1976)
facts.body: A Soho newspaper in New York, in May 1976, published an article condemning dance halls for attracting "truly evil people" and preying on community innocence, claiming these places had "nothing to do with either" dancing or music. "these dance halls have brought to this neighborhood the truly evil people who work New York."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Vince Letty's Defense Against Bigotry (1976)
facts.body: In May 1976, music journalist Vince Letty responded to criticisms of disco by citing a New York Post article that mentioned discos "reportedly attract substantial numbers of Blacks, Hispanics, and homosexuals." Letty urged the "party people" to assert their rights against the "bigotry sexism and hypocrisy" of communities criticizing disco. "If there is a disco community and I believe there is, Blacks, Hispanics, and homosexuals are at its core."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Widespread Ubiquity (1976)
facts.body: By 1976, disco had become ubiquitous across the United States, making it impossible to avoid on radio or in record stores, even for those who disliked it. "you could go to just about any part of the United States and find a disco in 1976 right on into the 1980s."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: Dilution and Saturation Concerns (1976)
facts.body: A Tallahassee, Florida DJ commented in July 1976 that updating old standards like "Venus," "Volare," and "Strangers in the Night" with disco beats was monotonous and diluted disco's appeal, signaling "the road to saturation." "updating old standards like Venus, Volare, and Strangers in the Night with disco beats was monotonous."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)
facts.name: Disco

facts.title: George Steinbrenner's Morale Boost (1976)
facts.body: In 1976, New York Yankees owner George Steinbrenner ordered disco music to be played in the Yankees locker room as a means to lift team morale. "In 1976, New York Yankees owner, George Steinbrenner, ordered that disco music be pumped into the Yankees locker room to lift morale."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 1 - Disco Doesn't Suck (Encore)

facts.title: Don Letts DJ'd Reggae at the Roxy (1976–77) – Punk Fans Embraced the Anti-Establishment Bass Lines and "Musical Reportage"
facts.body: Don Letts, later an associate of the Clash and a member of Big Audio Dynamite, was DJing only reggae at the Roxy club in 1976–77 to punk audiences. The punk crowd connected with reggae's "musical reportage quality" — the fact that songs were about something — the obvious anti-establishment stance, the bass lines, and the weed. This cross-pollination of punk and ska created the second wave. "Like minded spirits, you know, they were kind of reveled certainly on the streets of London that were thrown together as outsiders."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 1
facts.name: Ska

facts.title: Birth Year (1976)
facts.body: The punk explosion in 1976 is widely considered the birth year of Alt Rock, effectively setting in motion the alternative rock revolution. "If we look at the punk explosion in 1976 as the birth year of Alt Rock, 2026, which is when we're doing this, is more or less the 50th anniversary of this music."

facts.title: Starting Point (1976)
facts.body: The year 1976, marked by the "Great Punk Rock Explosion," is considered the starting point for alternative music, influencing practically all of today's alt rock. "Our starting point is 1976, the year of the Great Punk Rock Explosion, the thing from which practically all of today's alternative music emanates."

facts.body: RCA initially refused to release David Bowie's album "Low" because they did not consider it a guaranteed success, despite Bowie's prior consistent chart performance. They suggested he rework the album with more commercially viable hits.

facts.title: Career Origin from Sex Pistols Inspiration (December 1976)
facts.body: Inspired by the Sex Pistols' controversial TV appearance on December 1, 1976, computer operator Declan McManus quit his job, picked up a guitar, and changed his name to Elvis Costello. He wanted to embody the "attitude, the anger, the energy" of the Sex Pistols. "Shortly thereafter, an inspired Declan McManus quit his computer job, picked up a guitar, and changed his name to Elvis Costello."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Inspiration from Sex Pistols (December 2, 1976)
facts.body: Declan McManus, then a computer operator, was deeply inspired by the Sex Pistols' scandalous appearance on a TV show where they used "bad words." Feeling they had "shaken up the system," he decided to quit his data entry job, picked up a guitar, and changed his name to Elvis Costello, embodying the attitude, anger, and energy he saw in the Sex Pistols. "He wanted to be involved in whatever it was that the sex pistols embodied, the attitude, the anger, the energy."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Collaboration with Bowie on Low (1976)
facts.body: Brian Eno was instrumental in reworking David Bowie's existing ideas and rejected material from previous albums for "Low." He helped incorporate strong German influences from Krautrock bands like Kraftwerk, Neu!, and Cluster into the album's musical fabric. He was credited for his contributions to some songs and for production, though not as a composer for much of his work.

facts.title: VCR US Supreme Court Ruling (1976)
facts.body: A landmark 1976 US Supreme Court ruling affirmed the legality of devices such as Sony's VCRs. This decision established that such technologies were permissible because they enabled private copying of copyrighted material for personal use, setting a crucial precedent for future legal battles involving recording and playback devices. "Diamond Multimedia won the case based on a 1976 US Supreme Court ruling that made it okay for Sony to sell VCRs. That decision said that such devices were legal because they allowed for private copying of material, copying of material for private use."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: VCR US Supreme Court Ruling (1976)
facts.body: A landmark 1976 US Supreme Court ruling affirmed the legality of devices such as Sony's VCRs. This decision established that such technologies were permissible because they enabled private copying of copyrighted material for personal use, setting a crucial precedent for future legal battles involving recording and playback devices. "Diamond Multimedia won the case based on a 1976 US Supreme Court ruling that made it okay for Sony to sell VCRs. That decision said that such devices were legal because they allowed for private copying of material, copying of material for private use."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 2
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Early Punk Priestess Gig (1976)
facts.body: Patti Smith, described as a "punk priestess," played an influential show in New York City a couple of months before the Ramones' pivotal appearance in England. Her performance was an early, significant manifestation of the burgeoning punk rock phenomenon in the US. "Outside of a show, punk priestess Patty Smith had played a couple of months earlier, the Ramones appearance would be England's first proper exposure to US style punk rock."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: Patti Smith

facts.title: Sex Pistols Contract (1976)
facts.body: In 1976, EMI Records signed the Sex Pistols, placing them on the same label as established acts like Queen. This relationship facilitated the Sex Pistols' last-minute appearance on the *Today* show when Queen cancelled, as someone from EMI placed the call to get them to ITV headquarters. "At the time, the pistols were signed to EMI and the same label as Queen."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Cancelled "Today" Show Appearance (1976)
facts.body: Queen was scheduled to appear on the popular UK chat show *Today* on December 1st, 1976, as part of their pre-release press tour for *A Day at the Races*. However, singer Freddie Mercury "suddenly took ill" with a throat infection, forcing the band to cancel their live appearance. This cancellation opened the slot for the Sex Pistols, leading to their infamous, career-defining interview. "But singer Freddie Mercury suddenly took ill. It was a throat infection or something. And Queen, the band, had to cancel their appearance."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 10
facts.name: Queen

facts.title: Canceled "Today" Show Appearance (1976)
facts.body: Queen was originally booked as the guest for the "Today" chat show on December 1, 1976, but had to cancel because singer Freddie Mercury needed a trip to the dentist. Their marketing team suggested the Sex Pistols as a replacement. "The original guests were supposed to be another new group called Queen, but their singer, guy named Freddie Mercury, needed a trip to the dentist so they were forced to cancel."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 4
facts.name: Queen

facts.title: Cancelled TV Appearance (December 1, 1976)
facts.body: Queen was scheduled to be a guest on Bill Grundy's "Today" talk show on ITV on December 1, 1976. However, they had to cancel at the last minute, reportedly because Freddie Mercury needed to be rushed to the dentist for a bad toothache. Their cancellation led to the Sex Pistols being invited as a last-minute replacement. "But at the last second they had to cancel. Everybody seems to recall it was because somebody in the band needed to be rushed to the dentist with a bad toothache. I think it was Freddie Mercury."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Why Punk Happened
facts.name: Queen

facts.title: Loudest Band Record (1976)
facts.body: For an extended period, The Who held the record for being the loudest band, having been clocked at 126 decibels during a show in London on May 31, 1976. This sound level is significant as it reaches the threshold where physical pain begins for listeners. "On May 31, 1976, they were clocked at 126 decibels at a show in London."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Debut at 100 Club (1976)
facts.body: This new group made its debut at the 100 Club Punk Rock Festival on September 20, 1976. On the first night, their drummer savagely beat up a well-known music journalist, and on the second night, the same individual was arrested for throwing a beer glass, blinding a girl in one eye. This drummer was Sid Vicious, who would later join the Sex Pistols. "The lineup featured a new group called The Clash, a group making their debut called Susie in the Band Sheets, the Buzzcocks were there around a few others."

facts.title: Substance Abuse and Car Accidents (September 1976)
facts.body: In September 1976, during Labor Day weekend, founding member Gary Rossington was involved in a severe car accident while driving his new Ford Torino on Mandarin Road in Jacksonville, passing out behind the wheel due to excessive alcohol and cocaine use. He knocked down a telephone pole, careened off an oak tree, and smashed into a house, causing thousands of dollars in damage. The same weekend, bandmate Allen Collins crashed into a Volkswagen after his own drug and alcohol binge. Both were fined $5,000 by Ronnie Van Zant, who subsequently wrote a song about the incidents. "Gary Rosington, one of the founding members, was in a bad car accident over Labor Day weekend in September 1976. Too much alcohol and cocaine."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Introducing...Uncharted: The Lynyrd Skynyrd Plane Crash
facts.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd

facts.title: Assassination Attempt (December 1976)
facts.body: On the evening of December 3, 1976, around 8:30 PM, seven or eight armed men forcibly entered Bob Marley's house at 56 Hope Road outside of Kingston, Jamaica. Marley was shot twice, and his wife, manager, and a band employee also sustained gunshot wounds, though fortunately, no one died. The attack was reportedly orchestrated by elements within the Jamaican Labor Party (JLP) who perceived Marley as too politically progressive and influential, with some even suggesting CIA involvement. "Around 830 on the evening of December 3, 1976, 7 or 8 armed men burst into his house at 56 Hope Road outside of Kingston, Jamaica. Marley was shot twice."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Ed McCormick's Interview Impression (1976)
facts.body: In a 1976 interview for Rolling Stone, Ed McCormick described encountering Bob Marley "whacked out of his skull" and in a state of "deep and herbal meditation" while smoking a spliff at his Hope Road house in Kingston. "In fact, Marley was so whacked out of his skull that it was possible to study him in perfect Nubian carving profile for several seconds before even dawned on him that he had company."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 29 - Every Little Thing is Gonna Be All Right - The Influence of 70s Reggae
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Working-Class Origins & DIY Synths (1976)
facts.body: Paul Humphreys and Andy McCluskey, from the outskirts of Liverpool, couldn't afford expensive synthesizers. Paul, with a hobby in electronics, would scavenge old radios from relatives to create "noise making machines" that functioned as early, non-keyboard synthesizers, though their sounds were inconsistent. "We were actually playing synths because we couldn't afford one. We were playing all these noise. My hobby was electronics."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD
facts.name: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark

facts.title: Early Band Name: Hitler's Underpants (Pre-1976)
facts.body: Before OMD, the band members were in a group with the name "Hitler's Underpants," which they acknowledge as the "worst bad name ever." "This was before. I mean, I'm sorry. I once named that the worst bad name ever. Yeah, and it is. But we can confidently claim that once upon a time we were in Hitler's underpants."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD
facts.name: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark

facts.title: Marketing New Wave (1976)
facts.body: Facing radio resistance to "punk rock," Sire Records, under Seymour Stein, initiated a marketing campaign around Christmas 1976 urging the use of "New Wave" to describe their new signings, like the Ramones. This strategy successfully removed the punk stigma and propelled the term into mainstream acceptance. "So Sire launched a NAD campaign called Don't Call It Punk, urging people to call this new music New Wave."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave
facts.name: Sire Records

facts.body: At 16 in 1976, after moving back to Australia, he joined a band possibly called Dr. Dolphin with school friends Andrew Ferris (keyboards) and Gary Beers (bass), who remained his bandmates for life. His poetry was highly regarded, making him the group's lyricist. "In 1976, when he was 16 and after the family moved back to Australia, he fell in with a trio of school friends in a band that may have been called Dr. Dolphin."

facts.title: Androgynous Tuxedo Look (1976)
facts.body: In 1976, Grace Jones made history on the runway by appearing in a man's tuxedo for Yves Saint Laurent's collection. While initially regarded by some fashion critics as one of the most "unpleasant" images of the Paris runway, this look rapidly became an iconic moment in fashion history within two to three years. facts.title: Island Records Contract (Late 1976)
facts.body: Grace Jones signed her first record deal with Island Records in late 1976. This contract was initially a speculative venture, as she was a model transitioning into music, seeking to remain active in the entertainment industry. facts.title: Androgynous Tuxedo Look (1976)
facts.body: In 1976, Grace Jones made history on the runway by appearing in a man's tuxedo for Yves Saint Laurent's collection. While initially regarded by some fashion critics as one of the most "unpleasant" images of the Paris runway, this look rapidly became an iconic moment in fashion history within two to three years. facts.title: US Market Strategy and Live Presence (1976)
facts.body: In October 1976, while in Los Angeles for TV tapings, Benny Anderson stated that ABBA did not need the U.S. market, being already huge in Europe and Australia. He described their efforts to make it in the U.S. as "more for the sport and the challenge," emphasizing that they had no interest in being an opening act and had virtually no live music presence in the United States, aside from a few cities on their 1976 world tour, with Seattle being the first. "Benny Anderson made it clear that Abba did not need the United States. They were already huge in Europe and Australia by that time. They had no interest in being an opening act because it was not worth the time and the money and they didn't have a big enough audience in the United States to justify it."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 56 - Talk Shows of the 1970s
facts.name: ABBA

facts.title: Second Appearance on Dina (1976)
facts.body: ABBA made their second appearance on Dina Shore's talk show on November 26, 1976, where they performed two songs: "Fernando" and "Mamma Mia." "On their second appearance on Dina, on that November 26, 1976 episode, Abba performed two songs, Fernando, and the song that you that very well may have saved their pop music careers, Mamma Mia."

facts.title: Inspired by Sex Pistols Gig (1976)
facts.body: Future members of the Pet Shop Boys were present in the sparse audience at the Sex Pistols' influential gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4, 1976. Despite its low attendance, this concert became a crucial turning point for English rock, inspiring many who witnessed it. "In the audience that night were future members of the buscocks and the pet shop boys and joy division and new order."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Evolution from Jazz Fusion (1976)
facts.body: The band originally started as a jazz fusion band in 1976 before shifting towards a harder, louder, and faster sound, drawing inspiration from Black Sabbath and early punk rock. "They started out as a jazz fusion band in 1976, but they were also interested in groups like Black Sabbath and some of the punk rock that was starting to come out of New York and the UK."
